title: Capstone: combine patterns in a complete system
topics: Enum state model versus State pattern
objectives: Select Adapter, Strategy, and Facade responsibilities from concrete requirements, and identify where this integration simplifies their attached structures.
Distinguish the monitor's enum state model from the polymorphic State pattern taught in Chapter 19.
Turn a written contract into a tested C++17 program with clear data and ownership boundaries.
Trace and repair failures that cross conversion, state, rule, and history boundaries.
Add an independently tested rule while preserving established behavior and output.

sections.heading: Use the taught patterns to make specific decisions
paragraphs: This capstone is an original integration of earlier lessons, not another program from the attachments. Return to Chapter 6 for Adapter, Chapter 20 for Strategy, Chapter 10 for Facade, and Chapter 19 for the distinction between a state machine and the State pattern. The workshop scenario gives those ideas one shared call path: normalize a reading, apply the selected alert rule, commit accepted records, and produce a report.

The strongest direct pattern match is Strategy: Monitor owns an AlertRule, delegates classification to alert, and replaces that object without changing ingestion. AtLeast is the first concrete strategy; the lab adds OutsideBand. SampleAdapter preserves Adapter's translation responsibility as a value-conversion helper, without the attachment's Target inheritance or wrapped Adaptee object. ReportFacade preserves a simple reporting entry point, while its small subsystem consists of history access, counting, and formatting. These are deliberate reductions in structure, not evidence that a suggestive class name alone establishes a pattern.

Choose each boundary from the requirement that motivates it. Mixed units require translation; replaceable alert policies require an interchangeable operation; repeated reporting needs one formatting contract. The four lifecycle states need checked transitions, but their small behavior does not justify polymorphic state objects. Staging a vector before a swap supplies exception safety; it does not automatically introduce Command or Memento. The pattern-choice matrix makes both the selections and the omissions explicit.

sections.heading: The job: trust the whole path, not just the temperature formula
paragraphs: A small teaching workshop records temperatures from benches that use two sensor formats. Some readings arrive in degrees Celsius, marked C. Others arrive in degrees Fahrenheit, marked F. The operator starts a session, admits batches of readings, pauses to change the alert rule, resumes work, and stops the session. A report must show what the program accepted and what decision it made at that time. This is a teaching monitor, not equipment that protects people or controls a heater.

The hard part is not one calculation. It is keeping several promises together. A unit conversion must happen before a rule judges the temperature. An invalid batch must add nothing. A rule change must affect future readings without rewriting history. A stopped session must remain stopped. An object must not use a rule that has already been destroyed. The capstone joins these concerns in one complete program whose printed report is checked against an exact string.

The input is a vector of RawSample values supplied by the program. Each value contains an integer sequence identifier, a number, and a unit character. Identifiers must be positive and increase across the entire session, including within one batch. Accepted temperatures must lie from -40 through 125 Celsius, including both endpoints. The monitor stores at most eight readings so every full history is small enough to inspect. Empty batches are allowed only while running and change nothing.

We deliberately keep file reading, clocks, sensor drivers, threads, and network calls outside this program. They would add failure modes that hide the design lesson. A real integration can place those concerns before the adapter. It must define its own packet, timing, and recovery contracts. The complete C++ program here already has a useful boundary: either a supplied batch becomes accepted history in full, or the monitor keeps its old history.

sections.heading: Stage one: the useful ten-line idea and its first failures
paragraphs: The first reasonable design is a loop that compares each number with a limit and prints a label. If every input is valid Celsius and nothing must be remembered, that loop is enough. Do not start with an inheritance tree. Begin by stating the assumptions that make this small design correct: one known unit, one rule, no paused state, and no requirement to reject a whole batch together.

The excerpt below shows the first design. It is intentionally an incomplete illustration, not the delivered executable. With the Fahrenheit reading 100 F, it prints ALERT because 100 is greater than or equal to 80. But 100 F is about 37.8 C, which is below the intended 80 C limit. The comparison is mathematically valid and still answers the wrong question. The missing assumption is the unit of the value.

Adding a unit conversion inside the loop fixes this one error. Later a report and a replay tool also need the same conversion. Copying the formula into all three callers creates three places to disagree about unknown units and valid ranges. A named adapter now earns its place: it turns the outside representation into one internal Sample representation and checks the boundary once. Its purpose is agreement, not the extra class syntax.

The next failure appears when a batch contains a valid first item and a bad second item. Appending directly to live history leaves the first item stored even though the whole request is rejected. That result violates the batch contract. A temporary proposed history, followed by one commit step, fixes the actual problem. Only after these concrete failures do we introduce the larger structure in the finished program.
sections.code_label: Excerpt - first attempt; assumes every number is Celsius

sections.heading: Stage two: name the data before spreading behavior
paragraphs: RawSample and Sample are small data types with public fields. A raw sample still carries its unit. A normalized sample has a field named celsius, so later code does not need to guess. Record adds the decision made when that sample entered the monitor. Storing this decision matters: a later rule may classify the same number differently, but the old record is an account of what happened earlier.

The adapter first rejects nonpositive identifiers and nonfinite input values. A finite value is an ordinary bounded number rather than infinity or NaN. NaN means not a number. Ordinary comparisons with NaN do not behave like a simple out-of-range test: both NaN < -40 and NaN > 125 are false. That is why the program uses std::isfinite as well as comparisons. It checks the converted value too, because arithmetic on an extreme finite input can produce infinity.

For Fahrenheit, subtract 32, multiply by 5, then divide by 9. The constants have decimal points so the operations use floating-point arithmetic. Writing 5 / 9 first with two integer operands produces zero. Therefore (value - 32) * (5 / 9) produces zero for every ordinary finite value. The correct source keeps the intended order and floating-point operands visible. The uppercase letters C and F are the only supported tags; guessing a unit after receiving K would conceal a data error.

The allowed range is a program contract, not a claim about every real sensor. The boundary checks apply to the represented floating-point result. An outside device that needs tolerance near a physical limit requires a written tolerance policy and tests; silently adding a small epsilon can admit forbidden values. This example uses exact easy-to-check Fahrenheit cases, 176 F and 212 F, to test normalization to 80 C and 100 C.

sections.heading: Stage three: two real changes justify one replaceable rule
paragraphs: A fixed threshold is still a good implementation for a workshop with one permanent policy. Here the operator must change the policy between batches, and the lab adds a different kind of rule. If that change requires editing conversion, history, and reporting, the boundaries are wrong. We isolate the question that varies: given one normalized sample, should this reading be marked as an alert?

AlertRule describes that question through a virtual function. Virtual means the call chooses the implementation associated with the actual object at execution time. The compiler checks that AtLeast supplies a function with the declared shape; override asks it to catch a mismatch. The = 0 makes the base operation abstract: an AlertRule by itself has no answer. The monitor calls through the shared interface and does not inspect which concrete rule it owns.

The parameter const Sample& is a borrowed view of the existing sample, not a copied sample and not ownership of it. Const prevents changes to that sample through the parameter. The second const, after the parameter list, promises not to change ordinary fields of the rule through this call. Noexcept promises that this operation will not let an exception escape. It does not prove that a rule is correct or free from side effects. A rule that violates noexcept by throwing terminates the program; it does not produce an ordinary rejected batch.

The design contract therefore adds a behavioral rule: judging a sample must have no outside side effects. AtLeast merely compares two numbers and meets that promise. Logging from inside alert, incrementing an external counter, or sending a message would weaken the all-or-nothing story even if records rolled back. If rules later need historical context, change the interface deliberately and review how that context participates in a transaction. Do not hide new state behind mutable fields.

AtLeast stores an inclusive Celsius limit. A reading equal to the limit is an alert. Its constructor rejects a nonfinite or out-of-range limit before the rule can enter service. An alternative is a function object or std::function with a documented signature. That can be simpler for a few stateless policies. The explicit interface here makes ownership, replacement, and a separately named lab extension easy to inspect; it is not a demand that every comparison become polymorphic.

sections.heading: Stage four: permitted actions belong to an explicit state
paragraphs: Two booleans such as started and paused allow confusing combinations unless every caller is careful. A stopped flag adds still more combinations. A finite-state machine replaces that loose collection with one named state and a defined set of transitions. Finite means there are only a fixed number of possible states. Transition means a permitted change from one state to another after an action.

The monitor begins idle. Start moves idle to running. Pause moves running to paused. Resume moves paused to running. Stop moves either running or paused to stopped. Stopped is final for that object: create a new Monitor to begin another session. Ingest is legal only in running. Replacing the rule is legal in idle or paused. Reporting is a read operation and is permitted in any state.

Every transition checks its precondition before assigning state_. A precondition is something the caller must make true before the operation. Calling resume while idle throws a logic_error and leaves the state idle. A caller should not repair this by forcing the state field. The field is private precisely so a public operation remains the single place that enforces the rule.

An enum class and short member functions are sufficient here. The identifier State names an enum; this is not the polymorphic State pattern from Chapter 19 or the attachment's State, ConcreteStateA, and ConcreteStateB class family. Monitor checks state_ directly instead of delegating requests to a current state object. The State pattern becomes useful when each state has substantial independent behavior, many operations, or state-specific data. Our four states control only a few gates, and a class tree would make the program harder to follow. The state diagram describes behavior without dictating a particular implementation technique.

sections.heading: Stage five: validation, a proposed history, and a commit point
paragraphs: Monitor::ingest first checks running state and spare capacity. The capacity test subtracts the current record count from eight before comparing the incoming batch size. This is safe because every accepted history already has at most eight records. The operation then copies records_ into a local vector named staged. All further changes go to this proposed history while the real history remains available unchanged.

The range-based for loop reads one raw item at a time. In for (const auto& raw : batch), the colon means take each element from batch. Auto asks the compiler to infer the element type. The ampersand makes raw a reference to that element; const prevents this loop from changing it. Conversion returns a new Sample value called s. Each accepted identifier must exceed the last staged identifier, so the check catches both old duplicates and duplicates introduced earlier in this same batch.

After conversion and order checks, the monitor calls the rule and appends a Record to staged. Only when the loop finishes does records_.swap(staged) exchange the two vector contents. With the standard allocator used here, vector swap is nonthrowing. This is the commit point: before it, records_ is the old history; after it, records_ is the complete new history. The local staged vector then owns the old storage and destroys it when the function returns.

If copying, conversion, order validation, or appending throws before the swap, local cleanup destroys staged and records_ keeps its old contents. This is the strong exception guarantee for the monitor history: failure leaves the observable stored history unchanged. It is a form of rollback achieved by delaying changes, not by trying to undo half a loop. The supplied rules have no outside effects, so there is no external work to reverse.

The guarantee has limits. It does not make the program recover from termination, a process crash, or a defective rule that breaks its contract. It does not write durable records to disk. It does not undo a message sent by a future callback. Strong exception safety concerns ordinary C++ exception flow for the objects covered by the contract. Naming the scope of the promise prevents a useful local technique from being mistaken for a complete database transaction.

sections.heading: Stage six: ownership and reports without hidden lifetime traps
paragraphs: A Monitor owns exactly one rule through std::unique_ptr<AlertRule>. Ownership means responsibility for ending the resource lifetime. Unique means this pointer cannot be copied to create another owner. The constructor receives an owning pointer by value and moves it into rule_. std::move allows ownership transfer; it does not create a second rule. The monitor rejects a missing pointer so later calls need not repeatedly test for null.

The virtual destructor on AlertRule makes deletion through the base pointer reach the derived destructor. Replacing the owning pointer destroys the old rule after the replacement has passed the state and null checks. Destroying the Monitor destroys its remaining rule and its vector. The LifetimeRule used in checks borrows a flag that remains alive outside the monitor scope. Its destructor changes that flag, letting a test observe real cleanup without assuming that absence of a crash proves correctness.

A Monitor itself cannot be copied or moved. The four declarations ending in = delete make those operations compile-time errors. An automatic move would empty the old rule pointer while leaving the old state possibly running; calling ingest on that moved-from object could then follow a null pointer. For this session object, a fixed identity is the simpler contract. Moving a unique_ptr that owns a Monitor would still transfer its handle without moving the Monitor object. The type-trait static_assert checks verify these restrictions during compilation; they remain active regardless of NDEBUG. The small Sample and Record value types can still move safely because their fields preserve valid values.

ReportFacade supplies one simple request, summary, over history access, row formatting, and alert counting. It borrows a const Monitor for the duration of the call and returns an independent string. The caller need not know how rows are traversed or how counts are formed. A free function would be a reasonable equivalent for this small service. The facade earns its place as a reporting boundary; it does not own the monitor or repair invalid monitor state.

The records accessor returns a reference to the vector object. That avoids copying the history, but callers must respect its lifetime. Do not retain an element reference or iterator across ingest, because the commit can replace storage. A reference to the vector object itself still names records_, but its contents can change. The report uses only a short borrow and returns before any mutation. This single-threaded program does not protect a report from concurrent modification; introducing threads requires a separate synchronization design.

The report uses a classic locale and one digit after the decimal point. Locale describes formatting conventions, such as the decimal separator. Choosing it here keeps the displayed report stable across ordinary machine settings. The final output is not merely illustrative: main compares the generated string with the expected string and fails if they differ. A formatting change is therefore an intentional contract change with a visible test update.

sections.heading: Debug the integration by finding the earliest broken promise
paragraphs: Consider a wrong implementation that appends the converted first sample directly to records_, then rejects the second sample with an unknown unit. Before the call the history holds identifiers 1, 2, and 3. The submitted batch is {4, 21, C}, {5, 22, K}. The call throws, but the wrong history now ends at 4. A report would gain the row 4: 21.0 C ok and its record count would rise from three to four. The defect is the placement of mutation before full validation, not the wording of the exception.

Another error is rebuilding every Record::alert value after replacement. In the main scenario, reading 2 is 80 C and enters under a limit of 80. After changing the limit to 100, recomputing would print 2: 80.0 C ok and reduce the final alert count from two to one. That silently rewrites the earlier decision. The stored boolean is intentional historical data. If users want a second report that re-evaluates old samples, add it as a clearly named separate operation.

When diagnosing a failure, first write the expected state, count, last identifier, rule, and report before the action. Then trace conversion, order checks, classification, append, and commit. The first point where an invariant becomes false is more useful than the last line that crashes or prints the wrong number. A passing happy-path demonstration would miss both partial commit and rewritten history; the rejection and replacement checks exist to expose those failures.

The tests use check, which throws on a false condition. They do not use assert, whose checks can disappear in a release build when NDEBUG is defined. The rejects helper accepts a callable, runs it, and requires a logic_error-family exception. Invalid arguments and capacity errors belong to that family. Unexpected exception families still escape and fail the executable. These checks prove the listed cases, not every possible input or allocator failure.

sections.heading: What the compiler can prove and what execution must establish
paragraphs: The compiler verifies names, type relationships, access control, override compatibility, and the use of language syntax. It rejects an attempted copy of a unique_ptr owner. It knows that the declared rule operation is noexcept. It cannot prove that input identifiers arrive in increasing order or that a temperature is meaningful. Those depend on values that the program checks while running.

During execution, raw values enter the adapter, normalized values enter the rule, and completed records enter staged history. Control returns to ingest after each helper call. The heap-allocated concrete rule lives as long as its owning pointer keeps it. The temporary s lives for one loop iteration and is copied into a Record value before it disappears. The finished report owns its characters separately from the monitor.

For n stored records and b new samples, staging and processing take work proportional to n + b, with temporary storage proportional to n + b. A report takes work proportional to n. With the fixed capacity of eight, these costs are tightly bounded for this exercise. Removing the cap while submitting one reading at a time would repeatedly copy growing history and could cause quadratic total work. Measure against the workload before changing the design; a journal, chunked history, or a separate validated batch might support larger sessions with different tradeoffs.

The extension boundary is narrow on purpose. New unit formats belong in adaptation; new alert decisions belong behind AlertRule; new output formats belong beside the report service. A change to ordering, capacity, state rules, or transaction guarantees is a core behavior change and deserves wider tests. Patterns help only when they localize a real source of change. This capstone is complete at its stated boundary while leaving those larger system decisions visible.

example.title: A transactional workshop temperature monitor
requirements: Accept only positive increasing identifiers, C or F units, finite values, and normalized temperatures from -40 to 125 C inclusive.
Admit batches only while running; commit every record in a batch or none; permit an empty running batch.
Store at most eight records; preserve each intake decision through rule changes.
Permit rule replacement only when idle or paused; make stopped final; produce deterministic reports.
example.design: SampleAdapter applies the Adapter lesson through value conversion; Monitor and its replaceable AlertRule implement Strategy; ReportFacade centralizes the reporting request. A private staged vector supplies a single commit point. An enum and checked methods implement the four-state lifecycle without the polymorphic State pattern. No claim is made that this synthesized system appears in the attachments.
example.alternative: A single loop is better when all input is already valid Celsius and only one immediate comparison is needed. A free predicate can replace the virtual interface when policies have no separate lifetime or configuration needs. Direct append with compensating erasure is possible, but its rollback obligations become harder to audit as fields and failures grow.
invariants: The live history has at most eight valid Celsius samples with strictly increasing positive identifiers.
Every recorded alert is the decision made by the rule active when that sample was admitted.
A rejected batch or invalid state action leaves monitor state and stored history unchanged.
Every live Monitor has one owned nonnull rule; each rule answers without throwing or external side effects.
Monitor object identity is fixed: copy and move operations are deleted; transferring an owning handle does not move the object.

failures.mistake: Compare raw Fahrenheit numbers with the Celsius threshold.
failures.consequence: 100 F is marked ALERT at an 80 C threshold even though it is about 37.8 C.
failures.reason: The number was compared before its unit was normalized.

failures.mistake: Append to records_ inside the loop instead of staged.
failures.consequence: A batch with a valid identifier 4 followed by unit K throws but still adds record 4.
failures.reason: Live history changed before the entire request had passed its checks.

failures.mistake: Recompute old flags when replacing the rule.
failures.consequence: The printed main report changes record 2 from ALERT to ok and total alerts from 2 to 1.
failures.reason: The code confuses an intake decision with a new analysis of old readings.

failures.mistake: Use only lower and upper comparisons to reject bad numeric inputs.
failures.consequence: NaN escapes those range comparisons and may be stored.
failures.reason: Ordered comparisons with NaN are false; isfinite must be checked explicitly.

example.verification: Compile-time type-trait checks reject Monitor copying and moving. run_checks exercises missing rules, invalid limits, legal and illegal states, empty batches, both temperature endpoints, threshold equality, Fahrenheit conversion, cross-batch and within-batch duplicate rejection, late-item rollback, bad units, NaN, capacity, rule replacement, and destruction at replacement and scope exit. main additionally compares the exact complete report. These tests do not inject allocation failures, test concurrency, or establish suitability for protective equipment.
example.maintenance: The code gives future maintainers one location for input contracts, one rule interface, one state authority, one commit point, and one report format. Tests guard the interactions among those locations, where local changes can cause distant failures.

diagram.title: Who owns the rule, and who only reads the monitor?
diagram.explanation: Ownership points from the responsible owner to what it keeps alive. Inheritance points from AtLeast toward the interface it implements. The reporting dependency is a temporary borrow and carries no ownership. The concrete rule is held through the AlertRule pointer; the diagram does not mean the monitor owns two rule objects. Comments inside blocks are teaching annotations, not extra UML relationships.

extra_diagrams.title: Only these state changes are permitted
extra_diagrams.explanation: Each arrow is a permitted state transition caused by its named public operation. The absence of an outgoing stopped arrow is intentional. Intake and reports do not change state, so they are not drawn as transitions. Replacement is permitted in idle or paused and also leaves state unchanged. These states are enum values in one class, not subclasses.

extra_diagrams.title: One accepted item inside an all-or-nothing batch
extra_diagrams.explanation: Numbered call arrows show execution order for each item. Return values are described in the blocks rather than drawn as additional arrows. A conversion or identifier failure prevents later steps for that item. After every item succeeds, the monitor commits with records_.swap(staged). The diagram shows one iteration, not a separate transaction for each record.

focus.title: Normalize the unit before any policy decision
focus.what: This branch turns Fahrenheit into the internal Celsius scale and rejects any tag outside the two supported units. It changes only a local number, so no monitor history is at risk here.
focus.where: SampleAdapter::convert runs inside ingest before the order check and rule call. Identifier and finite-input checks occur immediately before this focused block; finite-result and physical-range checks follow it.
focus.why: A comparison cannot be meaningful until both numbers use the same unit. Keeping that conversion at the boundary prevents every future rule and formatter from having its own conversion policy.
focus.invariant: After the full converter returns, celsius is finite, in the accepted range, and carries the same positive identifier as the input. Unsupported tags must never be silently treated as Celsius.
focus.risk: Integer 5 / 9 would become zero. Omitting the unknown-unit branch would accept values with an unexplained scale. This excerpt is only the conversion branch, not the full validation contract.
explain: The comment states that units must be settled before judging the reading.
Copy the input number into a local double named c.
Compare the unit character with uppercase F and open that branch.
Subtract the Fahrenheit offset and apply the floating-point scale conversion.
If the unit was not F, test whether it is also not C.
Begin constructing and throwing an invalid_argument exception.
Provide the exception message and finish the throw statement.

focus.title: The replaceable decision contract
focus.what: The interface states the one decision that a rule must supply. It also makes deleting a derived rule through the base owning pointer safe. No specific threshold is stored in this base.
focus.where: Monitor stores an owning pointer to AlertRule. AtLeast derives from it, and the lab adds OutsideBand. Ingest calls this operation after conversion and ordering have succeeded.
focus.why: Changing the alert decision should not change unit conversion, state transitions, or commit behavior. A shared interface gives the monitor one stable call while the concrete decision varies.
focus.invariant: Each implementation must answer using the supplied valid sample without throwing or outside side effects. The virtual destructor must remain so ownership cleanup reaches the concrete type.
focus.risk: A missing override can leave a derived class abstract or select the wrong function signature. Noexcept is a promise, not a catch block; throwing from an implementation terminates the program.
explain: Declare the base class and open its definition.
Make the following interface members public.
The comment explains that cleanup must use the concrete object type.
Declare a virtual destructor and ask C++ to generate its usual behavior.
The comment documents the rule operation's exception promise.
Begin the virtual operation declaration, which returns a bool.
Borrow a constant Sample, keep the rule logically const, promise no escaping exceptions, and make this operation abstract.

focus.title: Ownership and state live in one authority
focus.start: // Own the rule and the record values.
focus.what: These private fields are the monitor's long-lived state. The owning pointer controls one rule lifetime, the vector owns stored values, and the enum names the current operating state.
focus.where: They are at the start of Monitor, before public operations. Constructors establish them; checked methods read or replace them. ReportFacade reaches history through a const accessor.
focus.why: Keeping the invariant-bearing fields private prevents callers from appending unchecked records or forcing an illegal state. One authority is easier to audit than unrelated globals or shared writable containers.
focus.invariant: A usable monitor has one nonnull owned rule, a valid state, and at most eight valid records in increasing order. The constructor and public methods jointly establish and preserve this contract.
focus.risk: A raw borrowed rule pointer could outlive its rule. Exposing a mutable records vector would let callers bypass capacity and conversion checks. Raising capacity affects the cost of each staged copy.
explain: The comment identifies which resources the monitor is responsible for keeping alive.
Declare the exclusive owning pointer to a rule through the base interface.
Declare a vector that owns Record values and its own storage.
Initialize the state field to idle when a monitor is constructed.
Define a compile-time size limit shared by all monitor objects.

focus.title: Guard a transition before changing state
focus.what: Start has one legal source state. The check rejects any other source before the state field changes, so a failed request leaves the machine where it was.
focus.where: This is a public Monitor member. Main calls it after construction, and run_checks also calls it from illegal states to verify rejection.
focus.why: A named operation keeps state rules beside the mutation they protect. Callers request an action rather than manufacturing a new enum value themselves.
focus.invariant: Only an idle monitor may enter running through start. A stopped object cannot restart, and a running object cannot be started twice.
focus.risk: Assigning running before checking idle destroys the evidence needed by the guard. Removing the guard would allow a stopped session to restart while retaining old history.
explain: Declare the start member with no parameters and open its body.
The comment states that the precondition must pass before any state change.
Check whether the current state differs from idle.
Begin throwing a logic_error to reject the action.
Provide the message explaining the missing precondition.
Close the rejection branch.
Enter running only after the check has passed.

focus.title: Prepare a candidate without altering accepted history
focus.what: A copy becomes the candidate history. Each new sample is normalized and checked against the most recent candidate record, so the same ordering rule covers both old and new items.
focus.where: This block follows state and capacity validation in ingest. Classification and staged append follow it; the final swap is outside the loop.
focus.why: Checking only records_.back() would miss a duplicate within the new batch. Checking staged.back() sees the accepted past plus every earlier proposed item without committing any of them.
focus.invariant: Before each iteration, staged contains valid increasing records. Before the final swap, records_ still holds exactly the original history, even if conversion or ordering rejects a later item.
focus.risk: Replacing staged with a reference to records_ would destroy isolation. Reading staged.back() without first testing empty would be invalid for the first reading in an empty session.
explain: The comment names the proposed history and its purpose.
Copy the live vector into a separate local vector; auto infers its type.
Borrow each raw element without changing it; the colon means take elements from batch.
Begin defining a constant local normalized sample s.
Call the adapter and use its returned value to initialize s.
First require the candidate history to be nonempty before using its last element.
Begin comparing the new identifier against the most recent candidate identifier.
Complete the comparison with the last candidate identifier and open the rejection branch.
Begin throwing a validation exception for broken ordering.
Finish the exception construction with its explanatory message.

focus.title: Store the intake decision, then commit once
focus.what: The chosen rule produces a boolean, a proposed record stores it, and one vector swap makes the completed batch visible. The flag becomes historical data at this point.
focus.where: This block is the end of ingest. The loop repeats classification and append for each valid sample; swap runs once after the loop ends successfully.
focus.why: Keeping the commit outside the loop gives a late rejection the same effect as an early rejection: no accepted history change. Storing the boolean prevents a later rule replacement from rewriting the past.
focus.invariant: Every staged record has been normalized, ordered, and classified. The live vector changes exactly once on success and never changes on an ordinary pre-commit exception.
focus.risk: Moving swap into the loop produces partial commits. Re-evaluating flags during reporting changes the meaning of history. Side effects inside alert would lie outside the vector rollback guarantee.
explain: The comment records the time at which the decision is made.
Call the currently owned rule and keep its answer in hot; the arrow accesses the pointed-to object.
Append a Record containing the sample value and its intake flag to the candidate history.
Close the loop after this item; further items repeat the same process.
The comment identifies the single point where a fully valid batch becomes accepted.
Swap vector contents so records_ owns the new history and staged owns the old one.

focus.title: A report borrows records and returns owned text
focus.what: The loop formats accepted values and counts their stored flags. It does not ask the current rule to judge old readings, and it does not change monitor state.
focus.where: This is inside ReportFacade::summary after stream formatting has been set. The method adds a final count line and returns the string after this focused block.
focus.why: One reporting entry point keeps unit labels, precision, row order, and alert counts consistent. A short const borrow avoids a full history copy without leaking a reference to report callers.
focus.invariant: Each row reflects a stored normalized sample and its original alert flag. Output order matches history order, and the resulting string owns its characters independently of the monitor.
focus.risk: Retaining an element reference for later use can become unsafe after ingest replaces vector storage. A report must not run concurrently with mutation without a synchronization contract.
explain: The comment explains that reporting reads without taking ownership.
Begin a range loop that borrows each Record without changing it.
Use the monitor history as the range and open the loop body.
Add one for an alert and zero otherwise; the conditional operator chooses between those values.
Write the sample identifier followed by a colon and a space.
Write the normalized temperature followed by its explicit Celsius unit label.
Choose the text ALERT or ok from the stored flag.
End the current output row with a newline character.

trace.state: Idle; zero records; owned AtLeast limit 80.0.
trace.reason: Construction checks the rule, then default member initialization sets idle.

trace.state: Running; identifiers 1 and 2 become 20.0 C ok and 80.0 C ALERT.
trace.reason: start permits intake; the adapter converts 176 F before the inclusive comparison.

trace.state: Paused; old records still have their old flags; new limit is 100.0.
trace.reason: pause creates a permitted point for replacement; ownership transfer destroys the old rule.

trace.state: Running; identifiers 3 and 4 become 90.0 C ok and 100.0 C ALERT.
trace.reason: resume permits a new batch; each new decision uses the replacement rule.

trace.state: Stopped; report has four records and two alerts.
trace.reason: stop prevents further intake; reporting borrows history without changing it.

summary: Apply Adapter's translation responsibility at the input boundary; the helper here is simpler than the attached object adapter.
Recognize Strategy in Monitor's replaceable AlertRule and delegated alert call; extend it with OutsideBand without editing ingestion.
Use the reporting Facade to keep one summary contract over history access, formatting, and counting.
Express this small state machine with an enum and checked transitions; it does not implement the polymorphic State pattern.
Delay observable mutation until a single commit point to give history a strong exception guarantee.
Separate ownership from borrowing, and treat intake decisions as historical facts.
Test boundary interactions and rejected operations, not only the final happy-path report.

exercises.prompt: In examples/ch23/main.cpp, change only the main demonstration's first AtLeast limit from 80.0 to 85.0. Keep the replacement limit 100.0 and every input unchanged. Update the wanted string so the program still verifies its output. Leave run_checks unchanged. What exact report changes?
exercises.hint: Record 2 enters under the first limit; record 4 enters under the replacement.
exercises.answer: Record 2 becomes "2: 80.0 C ok" and the final count becomes "records=4 alerts=1". The other rows and "checks: passed" remain unchanged. Change the wanted string in exactly those two places. The general checks still test the original 80.0 boundary and should remain valid; the demonstration is a separate scenario.

exercises.prompt: Start with Monitor m(std::make_unique<AtLeast>(50.0)); then execute m.start(); m.ingest({{1, 122.0, 'F'}}); m.pause(); m.replace_rule(std::make_unique<AtLeast>(60.0)); m.resume(); m.ingest({{2, 55.0, 'C'}});. Predict the exact string returned by ReportFacade::summary(m). Explain why the two flags differ.
exercises.hint: 122 F normalizes to 50 C, and stored flags are not recomputed.
exercises.answer:
The string is "1: 50.0 C ALERT
2: 55.0 C ok
records=2 alerts=1
". The first value equals the original inclusive limit of 50. The second is below the later limit of 60. Reporting may run while the monitor is running; it does not require stop.

exercises.prompt: A developer changes the adapter formula to c = (c - 32.0) * (5 / 9);. The monitor accepts identifier 1 with 212 F under AtLeast(80.0). What wrong row is printed, why, and how should the bug be repaired and checked?
exercises.hint: Inspect the types of the two operands inside parentheses.
exercises.answer: The wrong row is "1: 0.0 C ok" because integer division 5 / 9 yields zero before multiplication. Restore (c - 32.0) * 5.0 / 9.0, then verify 212 F becomes 100 C and alerts, and 32 F becomes 0 C and does not alert. The latter alone would pass even with the bug, so a test only at freezing is insufficient.

exercises.prompt: A new report needs CSV text for the same accepted records. Choose among adding CSV generation to SampleAdapter, adding a report operation, or adding a new AlertRule. Explain where it belongs and what must be tested. No disk writes are required.
exercises.hint: Ask which existing boundary already converts accepted data into a presentation format.
exercises.answer: Add a report operation, either in ReportFacade or a neighboring formatter, that returns a string. The adapter deals with external sensor representation, while the rule answers the alert question; neither should know CSV layout. Test exact headers, row ordering, units, and stored alert flags, plus the empty-history output. Keep the existing summary test unchanged. A free csv_summary function is equally reasonable if reporting remains small.

exercises.prompt: Extend the adapter to accept lowercase c and f as exact aliases of C and F. Retain every existing rejection and range rule. List four new acceptance or rejection cases and explain where the code should change.
exercises.hint: Normalize the tag locally; do not spread case checks into Monitor or AlertRule.
exercises.answer: In convert, map c to C and f to F before the existing unit branch, or accept both cases in those two comparisons. Tests should accept 20 c as 20 C, accept 176 f as 80 C, reject 20 k, and reject a late bad lowercase-unit item without a partial commit. The main report and all current checks must still pass. A local explicit two-case mapping is clearer here than locale-sensitive character conversion.

exercises.prompt: A reviewer wants Observer notifications, command objects for all button actions, and a different subclass for every state. Give a reasoned response for this program, and identify one concrete future requirement that would justify each addition.
exercises.hint: An abstraction should buy a needed change boundary, not merely a pattern name.
exercises.answer: Keep the current direct calls and enum because there is one report consumer, no queued action history, and short state gates. Observer becomes useful when multiple independent consumers must react to committed batches; define notification failure after commit explicitly. Command objects become useful for a queue or replayable operator actions; do not promise undo of external sensor effects. State subclasses become useful when states acquire substantial separate behavior or data. A sound justification names both the new requirement and the new contracts it creates.

lab.task: Add OutsideBand as another AlertRule with finite low and high Celsius limits satisfying -40 <= low <= high <= 125. It must alert only below low or above high; both endpoints are acceptable. Preserve Monitor, adapter, state rules, original run_checks, and the exact original demonstration report. Add extension checks for invalid construction, both endpoints and adjacent outside values, a late invalid batch with rollback, replacement back to AtLeast while paused, and preservation of old OutsideBand flags. Add one extra final line: "extension checks: passed". The starter already runs and verifies the original system; implement the extension without weakening those checks.
checks: OutsideBand(20,60) classifies 19,20,60,61 C as alert, ok, ok, alert.
Reject reversed limits (60,20), a low below -40, a high above 125, and NaN.
After four accepted band records, reject {5,21,C},{6,9,K} without changing the entire report.
While paused, replace the band with AtLeast(100); admit 61 C afterward as ok while the old 61 C record remains alert.
OutsideBand(20,20) accepts exactly 20 C and alerts at 20.1 C.
Every original check and the original five-line report still pass; print the added extension confirmation after the original check confirmation.
lab.answer: The reference solution stores two validated limits and implements alert as s.celsius < low_ || s.celsius > high_. Strict comparisons make the band endpoints acceptable. A new check_extension function tests the new behavior and its interaction with rollback and replacement, then main runs both old and new suites. No Monitor changes are needed because the existing interface already describes the varying decision. The solution briefly retains a reference to the vector object, which remains alive, but never retains a reference to an element across a commit. A function-based rule wrapper could also satisfy the behavior; explain its ownership and error contract if choosing that design.

glossary.definition: The operation that makes a fully prepared change visible as the new accepted state.
For the stated objects and ordinary exception flow, a failed operation leaves their observable state unchanged.
A value converted into the one representation the internal program agrees to use.
The decision stored when data is admitted, preserved even if later policy changes.
A fixed set of named states with explicit rules for permitted changes between them.
A check that old required behavior still works after a change.

problem_title: Build a workshop monitor that can survive change

attachment_alignment.epub_section: Integration of Adapter, Strategy, and Facade; explicit comparison with State. This capstone is synthesized for the book and has no separate attached chapter or C++ source file.
attachment_alignment.intent: Combine selected patterns around one program contract while showing exactly which attached relationships survive. Adapter contributes representation translation, Strategy separates the varying classification algorithm, and Facade gives the report client one request. The enum lifecycle demonstrates when the State pattern can be left out.
attachment_alignment.mechanism: Monitor::ingest asks SampleAdapter::convert for a validated Celsius Sample, calls rule_->alert through the AlertRule interface, and appends the resulting decision to a private staged history. A final swap commits the batch. ReportFacade::summary later reads stored decisions. Replacement changes the owned strategy for future ingestion. State checks remain ordinary comparisons against an enum inside Monitor.

roles.responsibility: Translate an outside representation before a client applies its internal rules; this helper does not recreate the attached Target/Adaptee object relationship.
Own the selected algorithm and delegate the varying decision without checking the concrete rule type.

roles.example: AlertRule; AtLeast; OutsideBand in the lab
roles.responsibility: Give interchangeable algorithms the same call contract; concrete rules supply different classification behavior.
Give the client one useful reporting request; this small adaptation has no separate subsystem class pair.

roles.attached: State example: Context delegates requests to State subclasses
roles.example: enum class State and checked Monitor methods
roles.responsibility: Restrict permitted actions. The goal concerns state-dependent behavior, but the enum implementation deliberately omits the attached delegation mechanism.

attachment_alignment.source_walkthrough: There is no attached monitor implementation to trace. Compare the earlier programs before tracing this synthesis. The attached Adapter translates an incompatible request; Strategy's Context calls the selected strategy's doAlgorithm and can replace that strategy; Facade coordinates operations behind one entry point. In this capstone, an accepted 176 F reading becomes 80 C, then AtLeast(80) returns true and that decision is committed. Pausing allows replacement with AtLeast(100). A later 90 C sample returns false, while the stored 80 C decision remains true. ReportFacade prints the stored decisions. The lifecycle is checked by Monitor itself, unlike the attached State example's calls through a current State object.
attachment_alignment.adaptation: The workshop requirements, temperature data, bounded history, transaction staging, enum lifecycle, and exact report are new teaching material. Strategy retains the attachment's context/interface/concrete-algorithm structure. Adapter is reduced to conversion between value representations, and Facade is reduced to one report service. unique_ptr expresses exclusive rule ownership. The lab supplies the second business strategy so students can prove that classification can change without editing conversion, state checks, ingestion, or reporting. A copied staging vector is temporary work for exception safety, not an exposed undo snapshot or an implementation of every pattern covered earlier.
attachment_alignment.recognize: For each claimed pattern, point to a relationship and a call. For Strategy, identify rule_->alert and replace_rule. For the adapted Adapter responsibility, identify RawSample, Sample, and the translation between them. For Facade, identify the summary request and the details it hides. For State, explain why no current-state object or virtual state handler exists. Names, enums, and diagrams alone do not prove a pattern.

contrast.distinction: SampleAdapter changes the representation a caller can use. ReportFacade packages several reporting steps into one request. Conversion and a convenient entry point solve different problems.
The operator replaces the classification policy through AlertRule. Lifecycle gates are controlled by Monitor's enum. Policy variation does not turn AlertRule into a state object.
A temporary vector and swap prevent partial updates during one call. There is no retained undo history, opaque memento interface, caretaker, queued command, or command-specific reversal.

teach.action: Assign mixed units to translation, interchangeable classification to Strategy, and consistent reports to Facade. Ask which requirement would justify polymorphic state objects; none does here.
Follow 176 F into an 80 C Sample, through AtLeast(80), into staged history, through commit, and into summary. Identify the pattern responsibility at each relevant call.
Implement OutsideBand as an AlertRule, replace it while paused, and retain the original report checks. Explain why neither Monitor nor SampleAdapter requires a type switch.

checks.question: The source declares enum class State. Does that establish the State design pattern?
checks.answer: No. Monitor performs enum comparisons itself. The attached pattern delegates state-dependent requests to interchangeable State objects. This system needs only the simpler enum model.

checks.question: Which unchanged call admits an OutsideBand rule, and what must remain stable?
checks.answer: rule_->alert(s) dispatches through AlertRule. The signature, nonthrowing and side-effect-free contract, state gates, conversion rules, commit behavior, and historical decisions must remain stable.

checks.question: Would free functions named convert and summary invalidate these design responsibilities?
checks.answer: No. They could preserve translation and the reporting boundary. The present helper classes are conveniences; neither needs an inheritance hierarchy solely to resemble the attached examples.

pattern_choice_matrix.problem: C and F readings must reach every rule as validated Celsius values.
pattern_choice_matrix.simpler_alternative: Compare raw numbers directly, or use one free conversion function.
pattern_choice_matrix.reason: Direct comparison misclassifies 100 F against an 80 C limit; copied conversions can disagree. A shared free function remains an equally valid implementation. Target inheritance and a wrapped sensor are unnecessary for the supplied value inputs.

pattern_choice_matrix.decision: Select AlertRule with AtLeast and the lab's OutsideBand.
pattern_choice_matrix.problem: The operator changes the classification policy while preserving ingestion and old decisions.
pattern_choice_matrix.simpler_alternative: Keep one threshold comparison inside Monitor, or supply a callable.
pattern_choice_matrix.reason: One hard-coded threshold cannot express an outside-band policy without changing Monitor. A callable could satisfy the requirement; the interface makes configured rule objects, ownership, and independent extension explicit.

pattern_choice_matrix.problem: Clients need one consistent string over history traversal, row formatting, and alert counting.
pattern_choice_matrix.simpler_alternative: Repeat a report loop in each caller, or expose a free summary function.
pattern_choice_matrix.reason: Repeated loops distribute formatting and counting contracts. A free summary function would work as well; ReportFacade is a small service and does not justify inventing more subsystem classes.

pattern_choice_matrix.decision: Omit polymorphic State; select an enum state model.
pattern_choice_matrix.problem: Ingestion and rule replacement must occur only in permitted lifecycle states.
pattern_choice_matrix.simpler_alternative: Use independent started, paused, and stopped booleans.
pattern_choice_matrix.reason: Independent flags permit contradictory combinations. One enum and checked methods express the four states directly. State objects become useful only if substantial state-specific behavior or data grows.

pattern_choice_matrix.decision: Omit both; use staging and a final swap.
pattern_choice_matrix.problem: A late invalid item must leave the whole batch uncommitted.
pattern_choice_matrix.simpler_alternative: Append each item directly to live history.
pattern_choice_matrix.reason: Direct append leaves earlier items stored after a later rejection. A temporary proposed history solves that failure. The requirements contain no user undo, command queue, replay, or retained snapshots needing either pattern.

pattern_choice_matrix.pattern: Factory Method and Abstract Factory (Chapters 1 and 2)
pattern_choice_matrix.problem: main must construct a selected configured rule.
pattern_choice_matrix.simpler_alternative: Construct the rule with make_unique and inject it into Monitor.
pattern_choice_matrix.reason: The direct construction already works. No inherited workflow must select a product, and no coordinated product family exists. Runtime strategy replacement alone does not require a factory pattern.

pattern_choice_matrix.problem: The caller needs a report after chosen operations.
pattern_choice_matrix.reason: An explicit read satisfies the requirement. There are no independently registered listeners. Adding callbacks would create extra lifetime and side-effect obligations around a batch commit.

pattern_choice_matrix.problem: The system holds a flat history and applies one selected rule per sample.
pattern_choice_matrix.simpler_alternative: Use a vector of Record values and one AlertRule owner.
pattern_choice_matrix.reason: The existing representation fits. No nested part-whole query or independently stackable rule behavior is required. A more elaborate structure would introduce decisions the contract never asks the program to make.
